A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same cross-lingual transfer study. Their text, figures, tables, and supplementary material are readable. The supplementary tables in v2 are retained within v3's main text, allowing reliable matching despite substantial reformatting.

before.justification: v2 reports original CodeT5 transfer experiments across four tasks, source-language ranking evaluations, SHAP analyses, and supplementary sampling-size results.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds Llama 3.3 70B-Instruct code-generation experiments on MBXP, including execution-based scores and source-ranking analyses.

M1.justification: v3 adds an in-context transfer procedure using three source-language function examples before a target-language completion prompt. This extends v2's fine-tuning-only transfer framework. The existing CodeT5 procedure and proposed LightGBM/LambdaRank source selector, including its feature definitions, remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v3 adds MBXP function-body generation across ten source and ten target languages, expanding the study from four tasks to five. The existing CodeNet and XCodeEval task coverage is retained. This adds a distinct task and dataset, beyond merely another model configuration.

E2.justification: The source-ranking comparisons retain the LightGBM regression-based ranker and programming-language-history ranker. v3 extends this same comparator set to code generation. Zero-shot and monolingual controls also remain; changed comparator scores do not establish new comparison methods.

E3.justification: The added generation experiment uses Llama 3.3 70B-Instruct, three demonstrations, temperature 0.8, nearly 1,000 evaluation examples per language pair, and execution-based Pass@1. These substantially extend the evaluation protocol. Newly disclosed CodeT5 hyperparameters and splits do not establish changes to the original experiments.

E4.justification: v3 adds a larger-model few-shot generalization analysis and examines which features predict generation transfer. Its SHAP analyses also revise the evidence for the original tasks. Conversely, v2's supplementary Figure 5, testing sensitivity to training-sample size, is removed. The new generalization experiment changes task and transfer regime alongside model size.

E5.justification: Section 5.2 newly states that each source–target pair is evaluated once and acknowledges the resulting inability to assess run variability. This is a disclosure, not evidence of fewer runs. Mean and standard deviation across leave-one-target-language-out ranking evaluations were already reported in v2 and remain in v3.

E6.justification: v3 adds the generation results in Figure 3 and corresponding ranking and SHAP results. It also revises the original tasks' ranking scores and feature importances: the clone-detection ranker now exceeds the regressor in Figure 4, reversing v2 Figure 3. The original transfer heatmaps and supplementary score tables are retained, while sampling-size results are removed.

T1.justification: Neither version introduces original theorems or proofs. The feature definitions, ranking formulation, and SHAP subset explanation remain substantively unchanged. The added generation task and execution metric are experimental specifications rather than new mathematical theory.

C1.justification: The abstract, contributions, and conclusion expand the study to five tasks and add a claim that findings and performance-prediction gains generalize to contemporary large LLMs. v2 makes no such larger-model generalization claim. The main findings about Kotlin, JavaScript, and task-dependent transfer remain.

C2.justification: Section 4.4 adds explanations linking type expression to transferable semantic signals and literal overlap to generation anchors. The limitations expand discussion of model and architecture dependence and explicitly acknowledge single-run variability limitations. These are substantive additions beyond the retained interpretations of the four CodeT5 tasks.

D1.justification: v3 discloses learning rate 2e-5, batch size 8, 20 epochs, split construction, per-language clone-detection counts, and generation-serving details. Section 7 replaces promised code release with a reported repository link, while dropping the promise to release 58 checkpoints. Documentation also loses the complete sampling-condition sentence, which is visibly broken in v3.

R1.justification: v3 adds discussion of Cassano et al.'s MultiPL-T work and references for MBXP, MBPP, Llama 3, and TogetherAI. It removes references and background discussion concerning MultiPL-E and some code-translation work. The central positioning around broader language/task coverage and source-language prediction remains.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, limitations, and conclusion are substantially rewritten. Research questions move into the introduction, supplementary material is integrated into the main narrative, and consolidated findings become multiple local takeaway boxes. These are extensive structural and language changes beyond the added experiments.

P2.justification: v3 switches from a two-column format to a single-column journal layout and relocates supplementary tables into the main text. It adds a dataset-count table and generation heatmap, redraws and extends the ranking and SHAP figures, enlarges retained heatmaps, and removes the sampling-size plot.

improvement.justification: v3 adds useful execution-based evaluation, substantial reproducibility details, and clearer single-run limitations. However, its expanded claims are poorly reconciled with the evidence: Figure 3 gives Go zero-shot Pass@1 of 0.60 versus at most 0.51 for few-shot sources, and Figure 4 reverses the clone-detection ranking while the accompanying prose retains the old finding. The claimed replication also changes task and transfer regime, and the sampling analysis disappears. These gains and losses in support for central conclusions prevent a reliable net quality judgment.
